# Results and discussion

## Hydrodynamic validation and seasonal retention {#sec-hydro}

The hydrodynamic module reproduces tidal dynamics, propagation, and conservative transport (@fig-hydrodynamic-transport). Modelled tidal range agrees with observations across nine stations, with a systematic underestimation of ~0.2--0.3 m in the first 50 km attributable to constant Chézy friction within each section. This bias does not compromise salinity-based transport validation, which is well reproduced. Saltwater intrusion varies seasonally, with the 0.5 isohaline reaching ~64 km in the dry season and retreating to ~25 km in the wet season. Full calibration parameters and statistics are in Table S2.

![Hydrodynamic and conservative transport validation. *(a)* Riverbed depth (prescribed input). *(b)* Channel width (prescribed input). *(c)* Seasonal tidal range: per-cycle mean (lines) and 5--95% inter-cycle envelope (shading) for dry and rainy seasons, with observed tidal amplitudes at nine stations. *(d)* Seasonal salinity profiles: model median (lines) with 5--95% envelope (shading) and all individual observations.](../figures/fig02_hydrodynamic_validation){#fig-hydrodynamic-transport}

Simulated residence time ($RT$) shows strong seasonal contraction in the urban section and is plotted together with the bloom diagnostics in @fig-rt-control c to facilitate direct comparison. Urban-section $RT$ decreases from approximately 53 $\pm$ 15 d during the dry season to approximately 20 $\pm$ 6 d during the rainy season, corresponding to a 2.6-fold range across the >7-fold upstream discharge swing (28--210 m$^3$ s$^{-1}$).

## Biogeochemical validation and longitudinal gradients {#sec-spatial-patterns}

Longitudinal biogeochemical gradients reflect a consistent three-zone structure: a downstream marine-influenced zone, a highly reactive urban hotspot (km 70--100), and upstream freshwater-dominated conditions (@fig-longitudinal-validation).

![Longitudinal profile validation for nine biogeochemical state variables (3×3 grid). Model seasonal-mean profiles with 5--95% interval bands (orange = dry, blue = rainy) vs. all individual field observations, with urban corridor shading. Rows 1--2: water-quality variables validated against 2017--2018 fortnightly monitoring (circles). Row 3: carbonate-system variables ($pCO_2$, DIC, pH) validated against 2019--2020 longitudinal snapshot campaigns (squares).](../figures/fig03_longitudinal_profiles){#fig-longitudinal-validation}

For the main bloom-seasonality story, the key validation result is that the model reproduces the coupled urban bloom system: dry-season Chl-a, the NH$_4^+$ hotspot, and the DO sag are all captured with good spatial fidelity (@fig-longitudinal-validation; @tbl-validation-summary). Because carbonate variables were compared with 2019--2020 longitudinal snapshots rather than the simulated 2017--2018 period, they are interpreted here as pattern validation rather than year-specific hindcast skill. DSi gradients are reproduced qualitatively but with weaker magnitude skill, so silica is retained as contextual support rather than a headline validation variable. Agreement is weaker for NO$_3^-$ and wet-season PO$_4^{3-}$ magnitude, pointing to remaining uncertainty in nitrogen closure and phosphorus buffering. In the simulations, NH$_4^+$ dominates dissolved inorganic nitrogen within the urban corridor, consistent with untreated wastewater inputs, while observed downstream NO$_3^-$ appears somewhat higher than simulated values, suggesting unresolved nitrification pathways or additional oxidised nitrogen sources. Wet-season PO$_4^{3-}$ overestimation is consistent with incomplete representation of monsoon-driven sorption--desorption dynamics [@NguyenNgocTuyet2019a] and macrophyte uptake in the urban canal network. Expanded monitoring-era statistics for the non-carbonate variables are compiled in Table S4.

Dry-season Chl-a at Bach Dang (km 70) is reproduced at $37$ $\mu$g L$^{-1}$ (PBIAS $-1$%), with the highest simulated biomass confined to the urban corridor and peaking near km 76 (@fig-longitudinal-validation). During the wet season, Chl-a at Bach Dang is simulated at $6$ $\mu$g L$^{-1}$ compared with an observed value of $5$ $\mu$g L$^{-1}$ (PBIAS $+8$%). The simulated dry-to-wet seasonal contrast of approximately 6.5:1 closely reproduces the observed sevenfold contrast ($37 / 5$). The modelled dry-season bloom is dominated by the diatom state variable, consistent with field observations of diatom dominance during high-biomass periods [@NguyenTruongAn2022a].

Temporal validation at three monitoring stations confirms that the model captures the main seasonal dynamics over 2017--2018 (@fig-temporal-grid). DO resolves the urban dry-season sag, Chl-a captures the bloom pulse at urban stations, and nutrient concentrations follow the seasonal enrichment cycle. Simulated wet-season nutrient concentrations remain somewhat elevated in the urban corridor, likely because the seasonal wastewater dilution signal is prescribed rather than dynamically linked to rainfall-runoff within the canal system. The remaining PO$_4^{3-}$ mismatch is also consistent with unresolved sediment sorption hysteresis and possible uptake by floating macrophytes in the urban canal network, neither of which is represented explicitly.

Each panel shows the hourly simulated time series against CARE discrete observations (red circles). Dry-season periods are shaded.](../figures/fig04_temporal_dynamics){#fig-temporal-grid}

## Residence-time control on seasonal bloom expression {#sec-growth-flushing}

### Damköhler analysis and bloom threshold

![Residence-time control on urban-section phytoplankton bloom dynamics. *(a)* Time series of urban-section residence time (blue line, 25-day rolling mean; shading shows $\pm 1$ rolling standard deviation) and monthly-mean chlorophyll-$a$ (grey bars). *(b)* Daily $RT$ vs Chl-$a$ scatter (small points: daily data; large points: monthly means) with logistic threshold fit ($RT_{crit} = 31.8$ d); grey shading shows the block-bootstrap 95% confidence interval and the dotted vertical line marks $RT_{crit}$. *(c)* Seasonal forcing amplitude comparison (ratio of dry-season to rainy-season means): $RT$ and $Q_{upstream}$ each show $\approx 2.6\times$ seasonal amplitude versus temperature (1.0$\times$), PAR (1.1$\times$), and dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN; 1.0$\times$). *(d)* Section--season Damköhler--$RT$ regime diagram: marker shape indicates estuary section (triangle-up = upstream, square = urban, triangle-down = downstream), colour indicates season (orange = dry, blue = rainy), and marker size is proportional to mean Chl-$a$; dashed lines mark $RT_{crit} = 31.8$ d and $Da = 1$.](../figures/fig05_rt_control){#fig-rt-control}

During the dry season, the urban section (km 70--100) achieves mean $Da = 33.4$ ($\mu_{net} = 0.63$ d$^{-1}$, $RT \approx 53$ d), with phytoplankton biomass peaking near km 76 (@fig-rt-control d). The upstream section also exhibits positive $Da$ in the dry season ($Da = 16.1$; $\mu_{net} = 0.41$ d$^{-1}$, $RT \approx 34$ d), yet Chl-a remains low ($2.1$ $\mu$g L$^{-1}$). This apparent inconsistency is explained by channel geometry: the shallower upstream channel (mean depth 10 m vs. 19 m urban) imposes depth-normalised benthic losses of 0.60 d$^{-1}$, nearly double the urban value (0.32 d$^{-1}$), which suppresses biomass accumulation despite positive $Da$. The ~10 m depth drop near km 60 (Dong Nai confluence) acts as a potential critical-depth barrier: in deeper, more turbid water, the ratio of mixing depth to euphotic depth ($H/Z_{eu}$) increases sharply, and blooms initiated in shallower upstream reaches may be inhibited when transported into this darker section. The downstream zone is loss-dominated ($Da = -25.1$; $\mu_{net} = -0.74$ d$^{-1}$, $RT \approx 33$ d). In the rainy season, the urban mean declines to $Da = 0.6$ ($\mu_{net} \approx -0.02$ d$^{-1}$, $RT \approx 20$ d), consistent with bloom suppression.

The phase diagram of simulated Chl-a versus $RT$ shows a clear threshold at $RT_{crit} = 31.8$ d (block-bootstrap 95% CI: 30.8--32.6 d; @fig-rt-control b). Figure S10 provides the full bootstrap distribution. The threshold is a property of the calibrated model rather than a directly observed quantity: below it, simulated biomass remains low, whereas above it, higher Chl-a values cluster along the dry-season branch. The seasonal forcing amplitude of $RT$ and $Q_{upstream}$ ($2.6\times$) far exceeds that of temperature, PAR, and upstream DIN concentration (@fig-rt-control c), confirming that hydrodynamic forcing is the dominant seasonal modulator. This sharp transition supports the theoretical framework proposed by @LiuBo2015, whose idealized estuarine models predicted distinct bloom and no-bloom regimes governed by the dimensionless ratio of flushing to growth. Our transient $Da$ analysis validates this theoretical regime shift in a highly complex, real-world megacity estuary.

### Hydraulic retention as the proximate bloom control

In this study, seasonal bloom expression in the Saigon River Estuary was governed primarily by hydraulic residence time rather than by seasonal nutrient delivery. Three lines of evidence converge on that interpretation. The Damköhler analysis identifies a physically interpretable threshold between bloom-suppressive flushing and bloom-permissive retention. SHAP attribution reveals a spatial partition between hydrodynamic and nutrient controls that mirrors the retention structure of the estuary. Structural tests further show that the model response depends most strongly on light-climate, loss-process, and organic-matter terms rather than on a simple seasonal nutrient trigger. The underlying growth-versus-dilution logic is consistent with classic river studies [@GarnierJosette1995], but in tropical systems it is easier to isolate because seasonal low temperature and light do not impose the same metabolic shutdown. Indeed, our quantitative Damköhler threshold provides a mechanistic framework for the field observations of @CostaL.S.2009, who found that high flushing in tropical estuaries physically selects against biomass accumulation and forces a shift in phytoplankton functional groups, regardless of nutrient availability.

### Mechanistic basis of the urban bloom window

The model diagnoses strong light limitation across most of the estuary, with nutrient limitation comparatively weaker (Fig. S5). Consistently, $\pm 50$% perturbations of the effective nitrogen uptake parameter preserve both the dry-to-wet bloom contrast and the spatial confinement of the bloom to the urban corridor (Table S11). Moderate NO$_3^-$ and PO$_4^{3-}$ mismatches therefore add uncertainty to the exact seasonal rate balance, but they do not overturn the threshold result because the seasonal shift in residence time changes the balance between net growth and export far more strongly than the observed nutrient biases change the Monod terms. The Saigon is thus an extreme tropical case in which hydrodynamic confinement determines when chronic nutrient enrichment manifests as intense eutrophication. Specifically, our model's diagnosis of severe wet-season light limitation perfectly mirrors empirical observations in Jakarta Bay, where monsoon-driven turbidity successfully suppresses blooms despite extreme, year-round megacity nutrient loading [@DamarArio2019].

The threshold behaviour emerges from three reinforcing controls. First, monsoon discharge shortens urban residence time from approximately 53 d to 20 d, shifting the system from bloom-permissive to bloom-suppressive conditions as flushing overtakes net growth [@LiuBo2015; @LucasLisaV.2009; @SunDetong2022]. Second, the dry-season bloom is sustained primarily by *in situ* accumulation within the urban corridor rather than by tributary inoculation: canals deliver nutrient-rich but low-biomass water, and removing tributary phytoplankton exchange in the model does not suppress the urban bloom. Third, light limitation and benthic loss raise the residence-time requirement for biomass accumulation; shallow upstream reaches experience stronger depth-normalised benthic losses, while the Dong Nai confluence increases downstream flushing and helps maintain negative downstream $Da$ values, especially during the rainy season.

## Data-driven support from variance attribution (SHAP) {#sec-shap-results}

SHAP attribution provides an additional within-model test of the simulated phytoplankton regime at the three monitoring stations (@sec-shap-methodology; @fig-shap-attribution). Each bar segment in @fig-shap-attribution represents the share of phytoplankton variability explained by a predictor group, summing to 100% at each station.

![External-forcing attribution for simulated phytoplankton variability. *(a)* Relative importance of exogenous predictor groups at three monitoring stations after iterative VIF screening (13 retained features; @sec-shap-methodology). Each bar segment shows the share of simulated phytoplankton variability explained by that predictor group; individual-feature contributions are listed in Table S7. *(b)* Summed hydrodynamics-related SHAP contribution (units: $\ln(1 + \text{Phy}_1)$) vs. upstream discharge at Bach Dang (km 70, Urban), coloured by season.](../figures/fig_shap_attribution){#fig-shap-attribution}

At the two upstream bloom-forming stations (Bach Dang, km 70; Phu Cuong, km 114), hydrodynamics-related predictors dominate simulated phytoplankton variability (60% at Bach Dang, 62% at Phu Cuong), whereas at the downstream station Nha Be (km 44), nutrient loads account for the largest share (40%) and hydrodynamics contributes 37% (@fig-shap-attribution a). This spatial partition is consistent with the Damköhler interpretation: chronic nutrient excess is necessary, but hydrodynamic retention is the dominant control on whether blooms develop.

Lagged upstream discharge is the dominant individual predictor, with the strongest contributions occurring over 7--21 d windows. This lag structure closely matches the residence-time timescale inferred from the threshold analysis, linking antecedent hydrological conditions directly to bloom development. Hydrodynamic contributions are positive under low dry-season discharge and negative under higher rainy-season discharge, consistent with flushing-driven bloom suppression as flow increases (@fig-shap-attribution b). Nutrient predictors remain important, especially near discharge sources, but they primarily modulate the magnitude of blooms in a system whose fundamental seasonal expression is dictated by physical transport, an increasingly recognized paradigm in tidal estuaries [@PaerlHansW.2006; @SmitsAdrianneP.2023]. Urban discharge itself was removed during collinearity screening, indicating that its temporal variability largely tracks the same monsoon forcing already captured by upstream discharge terms rather than acting as an independent seasonal driver. The comparatively low SHAP importance of light-related predictors should therefore be interpreted carefully: light limitation is severe, but much of its seasonal variability is already embedded in discharge through turbidity and residence-time effects. This resolves the apparent tension between the strong optical limitation diagnosed by the process model (Fig. S5) and the SHAP ranking, which instead asks which exogenous drivers best explain the timing of variability.

The limited cross-validated skill of exogenous-forcing surrogates at daily scale indicates that bloom variability is not fully predictable from external drivers alone. This is expected in a system where internal model dynamics, including nutrient recycling, effective grazing closures, and tidal mixing, shape day-to-day variability once the broader hydrodynamic envelope has been set. SHAP should therefore be read as seasonal-scale support for the mechanistic interpretation, not as a substitute for the process-based model.

## Carbonate response and CO$_2$ evasion {#sec-persistent-pco2}

![Carbon budget of the Saigon River Estuary. *(a)* Gross primary production (GPP, light bars) and community respiration (CR, dark bars) by section and season; horizontal tick marks indicate net ecosystem metabolism (NEM = GPP − CR). *(b)* Mean areal CO$_2$ air--water flux by section and season; annotation box shows the total area-weighted estuarine evasion.](../figures/fig06_carbon_reactor){#fig-carbon-reactor}

The carbonate module provides an integrative diagnostic of the same dry-season retention regime identified above. Simulated $pCO_2$ in the urban corridor regularly exceeds 10,000 $\mu$atm throughout the year, and total estuarine CO$_2$ evasion is 142.9 Gg C yr$^{-1}$ from area-weighted integration of section-mean areal fluxes over the 2017--2018 simulation period (@tbl-co2-budget). This value should be interpreted as a central model estimate rather than an exact inventory because gas-transfer parameterisation and the temporally offset carbonate validation remain important uncertainty sources. Net ecosystem metabolism (NEM) is negative in all sections (@fig-carbon-reactor a); in the urban dry season, depth-integrated gross primary production (GPP, phytoplankton only; no periphyton or macrophytes are represented) reaches $445$ mmol C m$^{-2}$ d$^{-1}$, total community respiration reaches $800$ mmol C m$^{-2}$ d$^{-1}$, and NEM equals $-355$ mmol C m$^{-2}$ d$^{-1}$.

| Section | Area (km$^2$) | Dry GPP | Dry CR | Dry NEM | Wet NEM | Annual CO$_2$ flux |
|:--------|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Downstream (km 0--70) | 90.4 | 43 | 445 | $-402$ | $-405$ | 51.3 |
| Urban (km 70--100) | 17.8 | 445 | 800 | $-355$ | $-692$ | 64.2 |
| Upstream (km 100--202) | 13.8 | 21 | 349 | $-329$ | $-338$ | 27.5 |
| Estuary total | 122.1 | | | | | 142.9 |

: Carbon budget summary for the Saigon River Estuary (2017--2018 simulation). GPP, CR, and NEM in mmol C m$^{-2}$ d$^{-1}$ (seasonal means). Annual CO$_2$ flux in Gg C yr$^{-1}$ (area-weighted integration). {#tbl-co2-budget}

The carbonate response shows that the same retention regime that permits bloom development simultaneously permits sustained heterotrophic processing of wastewater-derived organic carbon. Persistent urban $pCO_2$ supersaturation ($>$ 10,000 $\mu$atm) and negative NEM are therefore not a separate phenomenon but a second manifestation of dry-season confinement. Comparable coupling between eutrophication, respiration, and elevated CO$_2$ has been documented in the Pearl River Estuary [@JiangNi2024]. The area-normalised evasion rate of $\sim$1,170 g C m$^{-2}$ yr$^{-1}$ ($\sim$97.5 mol C m$^{-2}$ yr$^{-1}$) places the Saigon among the most intense estuarine CO$_2$ sources globally [@BorgesA.V.2011; @LaruelleGoulvenG.2013].

## Cross-system context and management relevance {#sec-management}

The calculated $RT_{crit} \approx 32$ days is substantially higher than values reported for faster-flushing subtropical systems. For instance, in the St. Lucie Estuary, autochthonous blooms are actively suppressed when storm discharges drive residence times below a threshold of roughly 4 days [@PhlipsEdwardJ.2012], while similar washout occurs in its major tributary, Ten Mile Creek, when residence times fall to 1 day or less [@BadylakSusan2016]. Furthermore, 1D modeling of the subtropical Caloosahatchee River Estuary confirms that physical flushing rates directly dictate the location and magnitude of chlorophyll maxima [@SunDetong2022]. This large discrepancy highlights the profound influence of estuarine morphology on bloom thresholds. Systems like the St. Lucie and Ten Mile Creek are extremely shallow (depths generally <2.5 m) and highly illuminated, allowing for rapid daily growth. In contrast, the relatively high threshold in the Saigon River is characteristic of a deep, turbid, strongly mixed estuary. Specifically, as demonstrated by idealized modeling of the highly turbid Ems estuary [@LiuBo2018], suspended particulate matter drastically depresses the net specific growth rate ($\mu_{net}$). Viewed through our Damköhler framework ($Da = \mu_{net} \cdot RT$), because the critical residence time is inversely proportional to the net growth rate, a severely light-limited system mathematically demands a disproportionately longer residence time to allow this depressed growth to outpace advective flushing. The threshold is therefore system-specific rather than universal, but it still provides a practical benchmark for identifying when hydrodynamic conditions become bloom-permissive [@LucasLisaV.2009; @SunDetong2022]. While the exact numerical threshold varies, the underlying dominance of hydrodynamic confinement is broadly supported by empirical studies in other tropical systems, such as the Paraíba do Sul [@CostaL.S.2009], where river discharge similarly overrides spatial nutrient gradients to dictate ecosystem expression.

This interpretation suggests a first-order management implication: if dry-season blooms emerge only when residence time exceeds $RT_{crit}$, then dry-season flow augmentation from Dau Tieng Reservoir could in principle help suppress bloom expression. Because Dau Tieng is already operated to manage downstream salinity intrusion, any such release would also have to preserve the salinity barrier and competing municipal and agricultural water demands. The threshold should therefore be treated as a management benchmark rather than an operating rule: it identifies the hydrodynamic range over which wastewater-derived nutrient and carbon loads are most likely to be expressed as acute bloom and CO$_2$ episodes. Wastewater reduction nevertheless remains the durable solution, while hydraulic management is best viewed as a constrained interim complement [@PaerlHansW.2006]. The threshold dynamics identified in the Saigon River are highly relevant to other rapidly urbanizing, monsoon-driven systems in Southeast Asia. For example, in Jakarta Bay, Indonesia, untreated domestic wastewater creates similar chronic nutrient saturation, yet peak phytoplankton biomass is strictly confined to the dry season when flushing and turbidity subside [@DamarArio2019]. Therefore, the Damköhler framework applied here could serve as a valuable screening tool for estimating eutrophication risk across a much broader class of tropical megacity estuaries.

Transferability should nonetheless be bounded by system structure. The growth--flushing benchmark developed here is most likely to hold in estuaries that are (i) chronically nutrient-rich, (ii) strongly seasonal in discharge, (iii) sufficiently deep or turbid for light limitation and benthic losses to matter, and (iv) dominated by along-channel exchange rather than by persistent stratification or large lateral storage zones. The numerical value of $RT_{crit}$ should not be exported unchanged to shallow clear lagoons, salt-wedge estuaries with sustained vertical decoupling, or systems where grazing rather than flushing sets biomass accumulation.

## Limitations and outlook {#sec-limitations}

The model retains structural simplifications typical of depth-averaged 1D frameworks. It does not resolve episodic vertical stratification or lateral trapping in sub-channel networks, which 3D modeling studies have shown can significantly alter local oxygen depletion, benthic-pelagic coupling, and nutrient cycling [@PeinJohannes2021]. Consequently, the inferred threshold should be interpreted as an effective along-estuary metric for the main stem rather than a prediction of short-lived or highly localized subgrid events. Uncertainties also remain in nitrogen closure, wet-season phosphorus buffering, and the role of floating macrophytes, which are prominent in the system but not explicitly represented in the current framework. Furthermore, uncertainties in biological losses remain because explicit zooplankton and benthic diagenesis are omitted in favor of simplified mortality closures. In particular, the quadratic mortality closure cannot reproduce the functional response or seasonal variability of real grazer populations. This is a notable simplification, as recent studies emphasize that estuarine hydrodynamics and varying residence times actively govern not only the phytoplankton assemblages themselves, but also their top-down trophic interactions with zooplankton [@SmitsAdrianneP.2023]. Furthermore, sub-monthly discharge pulses or lateral exchange with tidal flats may influence wet-season loss rates. The weaker DSi skill may also affect the simulated balance between diatoms and non-diatoms even though it does not alter the broader dry-season bloom timing. Carbonate diagnostics further rely on 2019--2020 longitudinal snapshots, so they are better interpreted as pattern validation than as year-specific hindcast skill for 2017--2018. These limitations may shift secondary details of nutrient partitioning and seasonal rate structure, but they do not alter the central interpretation that bloom expression depends on whether hydraulic residence time allows net growth to exceed flushing. Priority next steps are therefore to couple the present framework to a more explicit benthic module, extend the greenhouse-gas budget beyond CO$_2$, test scenario-based flow allocation between the Saigon and Dong Nai branches, and evaluate simulated diatom/non-diatom succession against taxonomic observations. Future model iterations could also incorporate specific phytoplankton functional groups (e.g., Reynolds classification), which have been shown to be highly responsive to flushing intensity in tropical estuaries [@CostaL.S.2009].
